title: The Instruction Hierarchy: Training LLMs to Prioritize Privileged Instructions
artifacts_released: N - no code, data or model weights released; the fine-tuned GPT-3.5 Turbo models and the synthetic training data are internal to OpenAI and no repository or availability statement appears in the paper.
models_evaluated: GPT-3.5 Turbo (fine-tuned with SFT+RLHF on instruction-hierarchy data); GPT-3.5 Turbo baseline (capabilities-only fine-tune); GPT-3.5 Turbo baseline + explicit instruction-hierarchy system message; GPT-4 used as the automated judge/grader
datasets_benchmarks: TensorTrust Prompt Hijacking and TensorTrust Robustness / password extraction (Toyer et al.); Gandalf Game password-extraction dataset (Lakera AI); jailbreakchat.com jailbreaks (unsafe and allowed prompts); known ChatGPT jailbreaks; author-created held-out synthetic evaluations for closed-domain direct injection, user conflicting/non-conflicting instructions, indirect injection via browsing, indirect injection via tool returns, system-prompt probing and borderline allowed prompts. Sizes are not stated.
key_result: Training GPT-3.5 Turbo on synthetic instruction-hierarchy data improves robustness on every safety evaluation, with defense against system-prompt extraction improving by 63% over the capabilities-only baseline. It also generalizes to attack classes deliberately excluded from training (jailbreaks, password extraction, tool-use injection), with robustness gains of up to 34% (jailbreak robustness up over 30%), while capability benchmarks (TriviaQA, LAMBADA, HellaSwag) are unchanged.
baselines_compared: A capabilities-only fine-tuned GPT-3.5 Turbo (same recipe minus the instruction-hierarchy data), and that baseline augmented with a prompted system message that states the hierarchy explicitly; the trained hierarchy far outperforms the prompting baseline.
threat_model: Three-party setting (application builder, end user, third-party content). Adversaries are either the end user, who supplies text in the User Message to override developer System Message instructions or extract the system prompt, or a third party who plants instructions in tool outputs and web results the model retrieves. The attacker controls only text content at a lower privilege level than the instructions it is trying to override, with no access to model weights or the system message itself.
stated_limitations: Authors note regressions in over-refusal (models sometimes ignore or refuse benign lower-priority instructions), notably on System Message Probing Questions and Jailbreakchat with Allowed Prompts. They also state the current models train the LLM to never follow instructions during browsing/tool use (too coarse), cover only text and not image or audio modalities, and are 'likely still vulnerable to powerful adversarial attacks' absent explicit adversarial training.
technical_summary: Proposes the instruction hierarchy: an explicit privilege ordering over System Messages, User Messages, Model Outputs and Tool Outputs, so that an LLM treats lower-privileged text as data rather than as commands when the two conflict. Generates training data by two complementary routes -- decomposing compositional requests into aligned sub-instructions placed at lower levels (context distillation), and using red-teamer LLMs to synthesize misaligned instructions the model is trained to behave as if it never saw -- then fine-tunes GPT-3.5 Turbo with SFT and RLHF. Evaluates on open-source and novel benchmarks spanning direct injection, indirect injection via browsing and tools, system-prompt extraction, jailbreaks and over-refusal. Matters because it reframes prompt injection as a missing privilege abstraction rather than a filtering problem, and is the training-time defense that OpenAI shipped and that later work (StruQ, SecAlign) treats as the reference point.

title: Transferable Direct Prompt Injection via Activation-Guided MCMC Sampling
artifacts_released: N - no code or data release statement; the only GitHub mentions are citations to GitHub Copilot
models_evaluated: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct; Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (both also used as surrogates); Qwen2-7B-Instruct; Llama-3-8B-Instruct; GPT-4o-mini
datasets_benchmarks: Tensor Trust attack dataset (attack samples from the online prompt-injection competition) for template construction; 33 human-expert injection templates drawn from StruQ; CYBERSECEVAL3 prompt-injection suite (251 tasks), 5 tasks for training and 2 held out for task transfer; 50 seed prompts per task
key_result: The activation-guided EBM + token-level MCMC attack reaches 49.6% average ASR across five mainstream LLMs, a 34.6% improvement over human-crafted prompts, and holds 36.6% ASR on unseen task scenarios. Transfer is markedly more stable than white-box baselines: attacking Llama-3.1, GCG-Inject collapses from 58.6% to 5.55% ASR while this method holds 71.6% -> 44.4%; human prompts score 0% on GPT-4o-mini while the generated prompts still succeed. Generated prompts keep low perplexity (PPL=127.68), evading PPL-based filters.
baselines_compared: Human-expert manual prompts; unoptimized initial prompts; white-box GCG-Inject (Zou et al. 2023); gray-box AutoDAN-GA-Inject (Liu et al. 2024); black-box PromptFuzz (Yu et al. 2024)
threat_model: Black-box attacker with only user-facing input access to the victim LLM application (direct prompt injection), no gradients, logits or query access to the victim; the attacker does hold a local white-box surrogate LLM (Qwen2.5-7B / Llama-3.1-8B) from which internal activations are harvested to train the energy-based scorer. The goal is to override the application's system prompt and hijack its task.
stated_limitations: Authors note a trade-off between prompt naturalness and attack strength (current PPL=127.68 is acceptable but stronger attacks would cost naturalness), and that the method does not attempt to evade text-classifier-based defenses, leaving detection evasion to future work.
technical_summary: Proposes a gradient-free, transferable direct prompt injection attack that needs no access to the victim model. Builds a template dataset by decomposing human attack prompts from Tensor Trust and StruQ into recombinable components (augmented with GPT-4o-mini), then trains an energy-based model over interpretable internal activations of a white-box surrogate LLM to score candidate adversarial prompts. Uses token-level MCMC sampling guided by that EBM to adaptively optimize natural-language injection prompts. Evaluates on five victim LLMs and seven CYBERSECEVAL3 task scenarios against white-, gray- and black-box baselines, reporting both ASR and cross-model transfer ASR plus an interpretability analysis linking activation patterns to attack success.

rq3.name: Activation-guided MCMC direct prompt injection (EBM-guided token-level MCMC; no acronym given)
rq3.note: Genuinely new and distinct attack-generation mechanism (surrogate-activation energy model steering MCMC prompt search for transferable black-box DPI), but the authors never give it an acronym or brand name, so the named-contribution bar is met only descriptively.

rq4.note: Attack paper; proposes no defense. Only discusses perplexity filters and text classifiers as evasion targets.

title: PhantomLint: Principled Detection of Hidden LLM Prompts in Structured Documents
artifacts_released: Y - open source tool at https://github.com/tobycmurray/phantom-lint
models_evaluated: None - PhantomLint is not LLM-based; it compares document text extraction (PyMuPDF/HTML) against OCR of the rendered region using a static bad-phrases list, so no LLM is evaluated
datasets_benchmarks: 26 author-built synthetic documents (16 PDF, 10 HTML) spanning the known text-hiding methods; all 3,257 accepted ICML 2025 papers from OpenReview (false-positive corpus); 119 curated real-world documents containing LLM prompts (113 hidden/positive, 6 visible/negative; 93 PDF, 26 HTML; CVs, arXiv preprints, theses, a book chapter, blogs, one email). 3,402 documents total.
key_result: PhantomLint detected the hidden prompt in all 26 synthetic documents across every hiding method tested (white text, invisible OCG ViewState /OFF, text render mode 3, off-CropBox and off-MediaBox placement, malicious blank-glyph fonts, HTML hidden visibility), and in all 113 real hidden-prompt documents, with no alarms on the 6 visible-prompt negatives. On 3,257 ICML 2025 papers it raised only 3 alarms, all OCR-failure false positives, giving a false-positive rate of approximately 0.092%. Mean runtime was 68.25 s per ICML paper and 43.75 s per real-world document.
baselines_compared: None - no competing detector is run head-to-head; the paper argues analytically that text-only prompt-injection detectors cannot distinguish visible from hidden instructions and so must produce false alarms, and it reimplements Xiong et al.'s malicious-font hiding method as an attack to defeat rather than as a defense baseline.
threat_model: A document author embeds LLM instructions in a PDF or HTML document so that they are invisible to a human reader but recovered by text extraction, in order to manipulate an LLM-assisted document-processing pipeline (peer review, resume screening, summarisation). The adversary controls document content and the hiding technique, is assumed to keep inventing new hiding methods, and the defender is the party ingesting untrusted documents.
stated_limitations: The authors note the detector works best when the suspicious text is short and occupies a tight visual region, since the OCR consistency test must isolate the smallest region containing it. They also report that the diffing implementation may not recover the entire hidden prompt and may highlight adjacent non-words such as punctuation or numbers, and that residual false positives are driven by OCR failures on non-English characters and very small fonts.
technical_summary: Proposes the first hiding-method-agnostic detector for hidden LLM prompts in structured documents, framed as a metamorphic test. Applies an ANALYZE step that flags text spans resembling LLM instructions, then an OCR consistency test that renders the minimal document region containing the suspicious block, OCRs it, and treats text present in extraction but absent from OCR as evidence of hiding; a detection requires the intersection of suspicious and hidden spans to be non-empty. Implements this in the PhantomLint prototype for PDF and HTML. Evaluates generality on 26 synthetic documents covering seven hiding techniques, false-positive rate on 3,257 ICML 2025 papers, practical utility on 119 curated real documents, and runtime.

rq3.note: Defense/detection paper. The hiding techniques it detects (white text, invisible OCG, render mode 3, off-page placement, malicious fonts) are all taken from prior work and news reports and reimplemented as test cases, not proposed as a new attack.

rq4.name: PhantomLint
rq4.note: Named, released ingestion-stage detector that compares extracted document text against OCR of the rendered region, making detection independent of the specific hiding method. Evaluated only against deliberately hidden adversarial prompts, not incidental degradation.

title: Misleading Large Language Models used (or misused) in Scientific Peer-Reviewing via Hidden Prompt-Injection Attacks
artifacts_released: Y - repository at https://github.com/Collins-115/TAISAP26 including a dataset of approximately 10,000 LLM-generated reviews and a demo video
models_evaluated: GPT-4o (primary, via the ChatGPT web interface with PDF upload); GPT-o3; Gemini-2.5-flash; Claude Sonnet 4; plus newer models released after submission, re-tested six months later
datasets_benchmarks: 26 papers rejected from ICLR 2024 (chosen because rejected papers are the hardest case for an 'Exploit' attack), later extended with 2 ICLR 2025 Oral (top 5%) accept-class papers; 4 representative reviewing prompts derived from an original user study with domain scholars; each query repeated at least 5 and usually 10 times (one evasion experiment alone totals 160 interactions). No public benchmark is used.
key_result: Hidden prompts injected into paper PDFs reliably steer commercial LLM reviewers: Ignore attacks succeeded in every trial against GPT-4o, Exploit-1 elicited a rating of 10 in 80% of cases and 9 in the remaining 20%, and Exploit-2 produced a rating of 9 in 97% of cases, all statistically significantly above the clean baseline (t-test, p<.05). Detect attacks were mixed (ASR 0.78 for the Cyrillic-character variant, 0.35 for the fabricated 'Collins theorem' variant; 0.17-0.93 across reviewing prompts). Obfuscation via keyword splitting and Cyrillic homoglyphs preserved most effectiveness (ASR 0.93 -> 0.79) while defeating keyword search, and explicitly instructing the LLM to disregard instructions in the PDF did not stop the attacks.
baselines_compared: Clean, unmodified versions of the same papers (baseline reviews and rating distributions, compared by t-test); and previously reported real-world hidden prompts found in arXiv preprints, which the authors show have no effect or are statistically inferior to their own prompts.
threat_model: The attacker is the author of the submitted paper, who can embed arbitrary invisible text in their own PDF but has no access to the reviewer's LLM, its system prompt, or the reviewing prompt. Three motivations are formalised: Ignore (make the LLM refuse to produce a review, discouraging illegitimate LLM use), Detect (force a recognisable artefact into the review to prove an LLM was used), and Exploit (obtain an undeservedly positive, accept-class review). A black-box variant assumes the attacker does not know which LLM the reviewer uses.
stated_limitations: The authors flag coverage as the main limitation: major experiments use only 26 papers (and some follow-ups only 2), queries were issued by hand through commercial web interfaces so the study could not be automated or exhaustively scaled, and they explicitly do not claim universal generalizability. They also concede their results are 'expected' given prior prompt-injection work, locating their novelty in the peer-review application domain rather than in a new mechanism.
technical_summary: Evaluates hidden prompt injection against commercial LLMs used to review scientific papers, formalising three author-side threat models (Ignore, Detect, Exploit) that do not all imply malicious intent. Derives four realistic reviewing prompts from a user study with domain scholars, injects invisible adversarial text (enriched with chat-markup tags designed to capture model attention) into 26 rejected ICLR 2024 PDFs, and measures attack success and rating shifts across reviewing prompts, papers and LLM families with 5-10 repetitions per query. Tests transferability to GPT-o3, Gemini-2.5-flash and Claude Sonnet 4, plus a black-box setting using multiple simultaneous injected prompts. Assesses detection countermeasures (keyword search, hidden-text detection, alternative PDF parsers) and evasion via keyword splitting, homoglyphs and translation, and reports negative results transparently in an appendix.

rq3.note: Systematic domain security assessment rather than a new mechanism. Hidden-text prompt injection in PDFs is taken from prior work and real-world arXiv incidents; Ignore/Detect/Exploit are attacker-goal categories, not named techniques, and the obfuscations used (keyword splitting, Cyrillic homoglyphs, translation) are standard. The authors themselves state their results are 'expected' and that the novelty is the application domain.

rq4.note: No defense is offered as a contribution. Detection approaches (keyword search, hidden-text detection, alternative PDF parsers) and a prompt-level mitigation (instructing the LLM to disregard PDF instructions) are analysed and tested only to show they are evadable or ineffective.

title: CAPTURE: Context-Aware Prompt Injection Testing and Robustness Enhancement
artifacts_released: N - the paper states only that the dataset generation pipeline code 'will be shared upon publication'; no repository link is given
models_evaluated: Guardrails evaluated: PromptGuard (Meta), Deepset, Fmops, ProtectAI v2, InjecGuard; LLM detectors: GPT-4o and Llama3.2-1B-Instruct; proposed model: CaptureGuard, three DeBERTaV3-base classifiers fine-tuned per domain (Python, Movies, Stocks)
datasets_benchmarks: Introduces the CAPTURE benchmark: MALICIOUS-GEN (context-aware attacks) and SAFE-GEN (benign over-defense probes) generated with GPT-4o across six application domains (Shopping, Covid, Movies, Stock, Travel, Python Code), seeded from public QA datasets with 30 train / 15 test / 15 validation base questions per domain expanded to 100 examples per domain per split. External benchmarks for generalization: NotInject, WildGuard, BIPIA (Injection).
key_result: Existing guardrails fail badly on context-aware attacks framed in an application's own domain: Fmops reaches 100% false negative rate while PromptGuard reaches 100% false positive rate, and InjecGuard and ProtectAI v2 show high FNR and FPR simultaneously. CaptureGuard, trained on CAPTURE-generated data, achieves near-zero FNR (0.00-0.15%) and FPR (0.00-2.05%) on the tested domains, and generalizes externally with 79.04% on NotInject (vs InjecGuard 87.32%), 75.00% on WildGuard (vs InjecGuard 76.11%) and 54.77% on BIPIA Injection, well above ProtectAI v2.
baselines_compared: Five off-the-shelf prompt guardrail models (PromptGuard, Deepset, Fmops, ProtectAI v2, InjecGuard) and two LLM-based detectors (GPT-4o, Llama3.2-1B-Instruct). Note that baseline numbers on the external NotInject/WildGuard/BIPIA benchmarks are taken from the InjecGuard paper rather than re-run by the authors.
threat_model: A user of an LLM application submits a single-turn prompt structured as Framework + Separator + Disruptor: a contextually plausible in-domain request, an instruction to disregard it, and the actual malicious payload (for example extracting the application's original instructions). The attacker knows the application's domain and conversational style but needs no model access. Indirect and multi-turn injection are explicitly out of scope.
stated_limitations: The authors restrict the study to direct, single-turn injections, excluding indirect and multi-turn vectors, and note attack diversity is bounded by the source QA datasets. They flag reliance on a single model, GPT-4o, as both data generator and evaluation baseline as a primary limitation that may bias the benchmark toward GPT-4o's stylistic patterns, and call for an ensemble of generator models.
technical_summary: Introduces CAPTURE, a generation framework and benchmark for testing prompt-injection guardrails under application-specific context rather than static attack lists. Builds attacks from the Framework/Separator/Disruptor decomposition of Liu et al., systematically varying each component with GPT-4o over six application domains, and pairs MALICIOUS-GEN adversarial prompts with SAFE-GEN benign prompts that contain trigger words in order to measure over-defense alongside detection. Evaluates five production guardrail models plus two LLM detectors, exposing simultaneous false-negative and false-positive failure modes. Then fine-tunes three domain-specific DeBERTaV3-base classifiers, CaptureGuard, on the generated data using InjecGuard's training recipe, and shows near-zero FNR and FPR in-domain with competitive transfer to NotInject, WildGuard and BIPIA.

rq3.note: Benchmark-generation paper. The attack structure is explicitly adopted from Liu et al. (Framework/Separator/Disruptor); CAPTURE scales and contextualises it via LLM generation but does not introduce a new named attack mechanism. MALICIOUS-GEN and SAFE-GEN are generation modes, not techniques.

rq4.name: CaptureGuard
rq4.note: Named guardrail classifier (DeBERTaV3-base fine-tuned per domain on CAPTURE data) evaluated head-to-head against five production guardrails. Conf is medium because it is largely a retraining of InjecGuard's recipe on new data rather than a new detection mechanism, and its contribution is entangled with the benchmark. The SAFE-GEN half measures over-defense on benign prompts, which is a false-positive study, not incidental context degradation.

title: BenchOverflow: Measuring Overflow in Large Language Models via Plain-Text Prompts
artifacts_released: N - no code or dataset release statement found; only an OpenReview forum link for the TMLR submission
models_evaluated: Open-source: Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, Qwen3-8B-Instruct, LLaMA-3.2-3B-Instruct, LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct, Gemma-3-4B-It, Gemma-2-9B-It. Closed-source: GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Flash, Claude-Sonnet. Nine models total.
datasets_benchmarks: Introduces BenchOverflow, a dataset of plain-text prompts spanning nine overflow-inducing strategies (including Implicit large enumeration, Explicit forced length, Change forms, Tokenizer stress, Infinite generation), built via a human-written meta-prompt template refined with GPT-4o and manual correction. Benign control is the OpenAssistant Conversations corpus (OASST2), adding 400 generations for a total of 4,000 generations under a fixed 5,000-new-token budget.
key_result: All nine plain-text strategies shift output-length distributions sharply rightward relative to the OASST2 benign baseline, producing heavy tails and frequent saturation of the 5,000-token cap; Explicit forced length and Tokenizer stress dominate CSR@5k. Overflow is reproducible within prompts but heterogeneous across families, with LLaMA variants correlating 69-71% within family while GPT-5 and Claude-Sonnet show the broadest cross-strategy associations. A generic conciseness reminder cuts mean output length by roughly 30% (GPT-5) up to 85-90% (Gemini-2.5-Flash, Qwen3-8B, Gemma-3-4B-It) and lowers CSR for most strategies, but Tokenizer stress remains comparatively resistant, so it is not sufficient alone.
baselines_compared: The benign OASST2 conversation corpus serves as the non-overflow control for length distributions and cap-saturation rates, and each model is measured with and without the conciseness-reminder intervention. Prior resource-exhaustion attacks (Engorgio, AutoDoS/CRABS, OverThink, BitHydra, Hidden Tail) are discussed in related work but not re-run.
threat_model: Deliberately weak: any ordinary user issuing natural-language requests, with no adversarial suffixes, jailbreaks, special tokens, model-specific artifacts, corpus control or model access. The paper frames Overflow as arising from helpfulness priors and absent length control, so it can be triggered inadvertently (student misuse, curiosity stress tests) or exploited at scale for compute amplification, cost inflation (denial-of-wallet) and cross-tenant service degradation.
stated_limitations: The authors note the study isolates plain-text prompt effects under fixed decoding and budget settings and does not cover tool-augmented agents, retrieval pipelines or training-time defenses; that proprietary results are point-in-time defaults that may change; that downstream task utility and user satisfaction under the mitigation are not measured; and that all models were run at their default temperature (1), which itself substantially affects sequence-length variance.
technical_summary: Introduces Overflow, a non-adversarial failure mode in which ordinary plain-text prompts elicit excessive generation, and BenchOverflow, a model-agnostic benchmark of nine prompting strategies that amplify output volume without adversarial suffixes or policy circumvention. Evaluates nine open- and closed-source models under a standardized protocol with a fixed 5,000-new-token budget, quantifying tail risk with cap-saturation rates (CSR@1k/3k/5k) and empirical CDFs, and analysing within-prompt variance and cross-model correlation. Positions Overflow against optimized resource-exhaustion attacks (Engorgio, AutoDoS, OverThink, BitHydra) by requiring no optimization or data control. Assesses a lightweight model-agnostic conciseness reminder as a first-line mitigation and shows it attenuates right tails unevenly across models and strategies.

rq3.name: Overflow
rq3.note: Names and characterises a distinct incidental degradation mechanism: benign, non-optimized natural-language prompts that saturate token budgets through helpfulness priors and weak length control, explicitly differentiated from optimized DoS attacks like Engorgio and AutoDoS. Conf medium because the contribution is delivered mainly as a benchmark and taxonomy of nine prompting strategies rather than a single new technique.

rq4.note: The only mitigation is an unnamed fixed conciseness reminder appended to the prompt, assessed as a lightweight probe and explicitly described by the authors as insufficient against the strongest strategies. It is not named or characterised as a defense contribution.

title: You've Changed: Detecting Modification of Black-Box Large Language Models
artifacts_released: N - no code, data or repository link appears in the paper
models_evaluated: Five OpenAI completion models (text-ada-001, text-babbage-001, text-curie-001, text-davinci-003, gpt-3.5-turbo-instruct) and Meta Llama 3 70B Instruct (used for the prompt-injection experiment)
datasets_benchmarks: No public benchmark. Author-generated corpora of short LLM texts, including three sets of 3,000 synthetic book reviews each (PI-0 clean, PI+ 'brightest and happiest', PI- 'darkest and saddest') from Llama 3 70B. Features include perplexity against a common reference model, dictionary-based psycholinguistic measures, simple linguistic features (word count, proportion of words over six characters), UMAP projections and UMAP over all-MiniLM-L6-v2 sentence embeddings; VADER compound sentiment annotates the review sets.
key_result: Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests over distributions of simple linguistic and psycholinguistic features reliably distinguish different LLMs behind an API without running benchmarks. In mixture experiments with text-davinci-003 and gpt-3.5-turbo-instruct, the method consistently detects a change in mixing fraction as small as 3% using total word count, or 4% using Bonferroni-corrected aggregated features. For the injection probe, appending a sentiment-steering instruction to the Llama 3 70B system prompt produces reviews that look individually unaltered but whose VADER sentiment distribution is separated by K-S tests.
baselines_compared: None - no competing detector is run. Benchmark-based evaluation, tinyBenchmarks and DetectGPT are discussed as alternatives in related work but not reimplemented or compared empirically.
threat_model: The defender is a downstream developer consuming a black-box LLM through an API with no visibility into provider-side changes. The 'adversary' is either a provider performing silent updates, model swaps, quantization changes or control-vector edits, or a party injecting text into the system prompt. The paper highlights a class of injection in which the target task is not replaced but a distributional property of responses (for example sentiment) is shifted, leaving individual responses looking normal.
stated_limitations: In a threats-to-validity section the authors concede the generated probe text is not task-specific, so merely knowing the LLM changed has limited value in many use cases and the method cannot identify the cause of an observed behavior change. They also acknowledge concentrating on a single model family (OpenAI GPT completion models), and note future work is needed on chat-based models, hyper-parameter changes and multiple open-weight models.
technical_summary: Proposes monitoring a black-box LLM for modification by comparing distributions of linguistic and psycholinguistic features of its generated text across time, using Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests (with Bonferroni correction when aggregating features) to decide whether two samples came from the same model. Evaluates discrimination across five OpenAI completion models, identifies which feature families carry the signal, and measures sensitivity on synthetic mixtures of text from two models. Extends the same machinery to a secondary question: whether a system-prompt injection that shifts the sentiment distribution rather than replacing the task can be detected, using 3,000 Llama 3 70B book reviews per condition and VADER sentiment. Frames the method as a cheap continuous alternative to benchmark re-evaluation, which is expensive and vulnerable to benchmark contamination.

rq3.note: Detection/monitoring paper. The injected prompts are two one-line synthetic sentiment probes used as a test stimulus. The authors do articulate a class of injection in which a response feature distribution is shifted rather than the task being replaced, but they neither name it nor develop it as a technique.

rq4.note: The monitoring method is never named or branded, and its primary target is provider-side silent model change rather than injection; prompt-injection detection is a single brief demonstration (RQ4 of the paper) with no attacker adaptation, no baseline and no deployment design.

title: The Defense Trilemma: Why Prompt Injection Defense Wrappers Fail?
artifacts_released: Y - full Lean 4 / Mathlib formalization at https://github.com/mbhatt1/stuff/tree/main/ManifoldProofs (46 files, approximately 360 theorems, no admitted proofs, three standard axioms)
models_evaluated: Live validation against gpt-5-mini-2025-08-07 and gpt-3.5-turbo-0125 with gpt-4.1-2025-04-14 as judge; alignment-surface characterisations reused from the Manifold of Failure framework for Llama-3-8B (mean alignment deviation 0.93, basin rate 93.9%), GPT-OSS-20B (0.73, 64.3%) and GPT-5-Mini (peak 0.50, basin rate 0%)
datasets_benchmarks: None - no standard benchmark. Evidence comes from MAP-Elites-generated 25x25 alignment-deviation grids per target model; the saturation study used 100 seed prompts plus 300 MAP-Elites iterations (400 evaluations, about 5,200 OpenAI API calls, roughly 130 minutes and $15) filling 82 cells, 66 strictly unsafe and 10 boundary.
key_result: Proves that no continuous, utility-preserving input wrapper D: X -> X can make all outputs safe on a connected prompt space, via three results of increasing strength: boundary fixation (some threshold-level input is passed through unchanged), an epsilon-robust constraint under Lipschitz regularity (f(D(x)) >= tau - LK*delta near the fixed boundary point), and, under transversality, a positive-measure region that stays strictly unsafe. Continuity, utility preservation and completeness cannot coexist. In three live runs the predicted persistent-unsafe set matched the actual post-defense unsafe set cell-for-cell with zero interior false positives.
baselines_compared: None - no defense is implemented or compared. The empirical check uses the canonical continuous defense D = identity (K=1) as the test instance, and the paper positions itself against other impossibility results in a related-work table rather than running them.
threat_model: Abstract rather than operational: prompts live in a connected metric space with a real-valued alignment-deviation function and a safety threshold tau. The defense is any continuous, utility-preserving preprocessing function applied before the model sees the input; the adversary needs only to find inputs near the safety boundary. Multi-turn interaction and stochastic defenses are covered by extensions, and parallel discrete results are proved without topology.
stated_limitations: The authors are explicit that the theorems cover only a single continuous, utility-preserving input wrapper and do not preclude training-time alignment (RLHF, DPO, constitutional AI), architectural changes, discontinuous defenses such as hard blocklists or discrete classifiers, output-side filters, ensembles, human-in-the-loop review, adaptive thresholds, or multi-component systems that reject or redirect inputs rather than preserving utility. One of their own falsifiable predictions is marked not directly tested for lack of a pipeline experiment.
technical_summary: Proves an impossibility result for prompt-injection defense wrappers: on a connected prompt space the safe region is open but not closed, so any continuous defense that fixes safe inputs must also fix a point on the safety boundary. Strengthens this to an epsilon-robust bound under Lipschitz regularity and, under a transversality condition, to a positive-measure region that remains strictly unsafe after defense, yielding a trilemma among continuity, utility preservation and completeness. Extends the results to multi-turn interaction, stochastic defenses, and to continuous interpolants of finite behavioral data via the Tietze extension theorem, with parallel discrete versions requiring no topology. Mechanically verifies the whole theory in Lean 4 with Mathlib and checks the central containment prediction live against two OpenAI models using MAP-Elites alignment-deviation grids.

rq3.note: Theory paper. No attack technique or degradation mechanism is proposed; prompt injection is treated abstractly as inputs whose alignment deviation exceeds a threshold.

rq4.note: Proves that a whole class of defenses (continuous, utility-preserving input wrappers) cannot be complete. It offers no defense of its own and explicitly lists the defense classes its result does not constrain.

title: Soft Begging: Modular and Efficient Shielding of LLMs against Prompt Injection and Jailbreaking based on Prompt Tuning
artifacts_released: N - no code, models or data; the paper is a three-page extended abstract with no artifact statement
models_evaluated: None - no experiments were run. The paper describes how prompt-injection defenses are normally evaluated but reports no model, run or number of its own.
datasets_benchmarks: None - no dataset is used. Existing indirect-injection benchmarks (Yi et al. 2024; Zhan et al., InjecAgent 2024) are cited as the kind of resource a future evaluation would use.
key_result: No quantitative result is reported. The paper's claims are conjectures: that parameter-level soft prompts should beat text-level counter-prompting, that training a soft prompt is orders of magnitude cheaper than fine-tuning the full model, and that per-attack soft prompts could be modularized and combined via prompt fusion.

technical_summary: Proposes InstruCoT, an instruction-level safety-alignment method that defends LLMs against prompt injection by (1) synthesizing a diverse training dataset spanning three threat scenarios (behavior deviation, privacy leakage, harmful output), multiple context-region injection positions, and (2) fine-tuning the LLM on chain-of-thought reasoning traces - inspired by Endsley's Situation Awareness model - that guide it to perceive all instructions in context, judge whether each violates the system prompt's scope, and decide which to follow or refuse. rq3.note: Introduces no new attack technique; synthesizes training data using existing injection styles/positions to build a defense, and evaluates against established threat categories (behavior deviation, privacy leakage, harmful output).

rq4.name: InstruCoT
rq4.note: Named, released (code+data), rigorously evaluated instruction-level CoT fine-tuning defense across 4 open LLMs, 3 threat dimensions, and multiple baselines with large, consistent Defense Rate improvements.

title: KVEraser: Learning to Steer KV Cache for Efficient Localized Context Erasing
artifacts_released: Y - implementation available at https://github.com/Graph-COM/KVEraser
models_evaluated: Qwen3-8B (32K-token context)
datasets_benchmarks: A controlled synthetic 'Erasing needle in a haystack' (NIAH) benchmark isolating post-hoc span deletion across 1K-32K context lengths, built from Natural Questions/HotpotQA/TriviaQA-style passages; and long-document QA with harmful factual distractors mined from non-gold Wikipedia pages, trained on one QA source and evaluated zero-shot on three unseen datasets (2WikiMultiHopQA, MuSiQue, IIRC)
key_result: On the controlled NIAH-style benchmark, KVEraser nearly matches full recomputation's post-erasure quality across 1K-32K context lengths while its latency increases only 24% versus a 17.6x latency increase for full recomputation; on unseen long-document QA with harmful distractors, KVEraser achieves the highest exact match among approximate baselines with a 3-4x speedup over full recomputation, landing on the quality-efficiency Pareto frontier where the strongest baseline (local suffix repair) trails in quality.
baselines_compared: Full recomputation (quality reference, high cost), delete-and-shift (with RoPE re-rotation), instruction-only forgetting (prompt-based selective forgetting per LLM memory-benchmark literature), and local suffix repair (partial suffix recomputation)
threat_model: N/A - not an adversarial-attack defense in the classic sense; the paper targets a general 'context erasing' problem where a short span already written into the KV cache is later identified as stale (out-of-date retrieved facts), incorrect (a faulty tool observation), retracted (a withdrawn user preference), or harmful (an adversarial instruction/injection in an imported skill file), and the system must make future decoding behave as though that span never appeared, without full recomputation.
stated_limitations: The authors frame the work as an initial step: a residual quality gap versus full recomputation remains on natural QA, which they attribute partly to the current training data's scale and diversity; scaling and diversifying the training data is left as future work. Only a single model (Qwen3-8B) and its own architecture-specific KV mechanics (RoPE) are evaluated; multi-span/iterative erasing is explicitly left to future work.
technical_summary: Introduces KVEraser, a learned KV-cache editing method that performs efficient, localized 'context erasing': given a processed context and a span to remove (e.g., a stale retrieved fact, an incorrect tool observation, a retracted user preference, or a harmful injected instruction), it replaces only that span's cached KV states with learned steering states while reusing the rest of the cache unchanged, avoiding the suffix-length-dependent cost of full recomputation. Trains a two-stage pipeline (generic span-neighbor pre-training, then task-specific fine-tuning) on Qwen3-8B and evaluates against full recomputation and three approximate baselines (delete-and-shift, instruction-only forgetting, local suffix repair) on a controlled synthetic erasing benchmark (1K-32K context) and on unseen long-document QA with harmful factual distractors, achieving near-full-recomputation quality at a fraction of the latency cost and the best quality-efficiency tradeoff among approximate methods.

rq3.note: No new attack technique; the harmful factual distractors used for evaluation are constructed via standard retrieval-based distractor mining, not a novel injection method.

rq4.name: KVEraser
rq4.note: Named, code-released, rigorously benchmarked KV-cache-editing mechanism for erasing problematic context spans; motivated in part by adversarial prompt injection but the paper's own quantitative evaluation tests erasure of harmful/misleading factual distractors in QA and a synthetic span-deletion benchmark, not an adversarial attack-success-rate evaluation, so validated_against is incidental rather than adversarial or both.

title: Counterfactual Evaluation for Blind Attack Detection in LLM-based Evaluation Systems
artifacts_released: N - no code or dataset release link is given (only the six third-party QA datasets used are cited as publicly available)
models_evaluated: GPT-3.5-turbo; GPT-4o-mini; GPT-4o; o1 (all via OpenAI API); Gemma (google/gemma-3-12b-it); LLaMA (meta/llama-3.1-8b-instruct); Mistral (mistralai/mistral-7b-instruct) via OpenRouter
datasets_benchmarks: Six English QA datasets sampled at 100 questions each (600 total): GSM8K, HotpotQA, SQuAD 1.1, StrategyQA, TriviaQA, TruthfulQA
key_result: Under Standard Evaluation (SE) alone, blind-attack submissions (a reworded restatement of the question in place of an answer) achieve attack success rates of 61.8% (GPT-3.5-turbo), 98.2% (GPT-4o-mini), 95.8% (GPT-4o), and 99.8% (o1); adding Counterfactual Evaluation (SE+CFE) raises attack-detection F1 to 97.8%, 95.8%, and 99.8% for GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4o, and o1 respectively (accuracy >96% for all three), while GPT-3.5-turbo improves more modestly (correct-detection F1 70.8%->82.8%, attack-detection F1 only 0.564); among open-source models, Gemma-12B reaches 89.3% accuracy under SE+CFE while LLaMA-8B underperforms.
baselines_compared: Standard Evaluation (SE) alone serves as the baseline/control condition against which the proposed SE+CFE framework is compared, across all seven LLMs and six datasets
threat_model: A 'blind attack': a candidate answer submitted to an LLM-based evaluator is crafted independently of the true ground-truth answer (e.g., simply rephrasing the question) so that it superficially resembles a valid response and gets accepted regardless of correctness, exploiting the evaluator LLM's tendency to hallucinate plausible-but-incorrect judgments; the attacker's goal is to fraudulently pass evaluation in an LLM-graded benchmark or competition without providing a genuinely correct answer.
stated_limitations: Experiments are confined to English benchmarks, so effectiveness in languages with richer morphology or different syntax may differ. The framework relies on a binary correct/incorrect judgment, a simplification given that real-world QA answers can be partially correct or take multiple valid forms. Evaluation is limited to standard, off-the-shelf LLMs; the authors note fine-tuning could further improve security but was not explored.
technical_summary: Formalizes 'blind attacks' against LLM-based evaluation systems, where a submitted candidate answer is crafted independently of the true answer (e.g., a reworded restatement of the question) to deceive an LLM judge into accepting it regardless of correctness. Proposes a defense framework combining Standard Evaluation (SE) with Counterfactual Evaluation (CFE), which re-runs the evaluation against a deliberately substituted false ground-truth answer; an attack is flagged when the submission is validated under both the true and the counterfactual ground truth, since blind attacks are invariant to this substitution while honest answers are not. Evaluates across six QA datasets and seven LLMs (four proprietary, three open-source), showing standard evaluation is highly vulnerable (attack success rates up to 99.8%) while SE+CFE substantially improves attack detection (F1 up to 99.8%) with minimal loss in benign-case accuracy, though weaker models like GPT-3.5-turbo and LLaMA-8B benefit less.

rq3.name: Blind attacks
rq3.note: Formally defines and names a new threat class against LLM-based evaluators: a candidate answer constructed independently of the ground truth to be accepted regardless of correctness, exploiting evaluator hallucination.

rq4.name: SE+CFE (Standard Evaluation + Counterfactual Evaluation)
rq4.note: Named, quantitatively validated detection framework tested across 6 datasets x 7 LLMs with a clear baseline (SE alone) and large, consistent F1 improvements for attack detection.

title: CLIOPATRA: Extracting Private Information from LLM Insights

An adversary inserts malicious chats that simultaneously defeat PII redaction, cluster with a target user's conversation, force the target's sensitive information into the generated cluster-summary insight, and obfuscate that leak to evade privacy auditors. rq3.name: Cliopatra
rq3.note: First named attack combining data poisoning, prompt injection, and attribute inference to break multi-layer heuristic privacy protections in LLM-based conversation-insight/aggregation systems (e.g., Clio), demonstrated with concrete, high attack success rates.

rq4.note: Attack-only paper; it evaluates the target system's own pre-existing LLM-based privacy auditor and finds it ineffective, and reports mitigations the target's authors say they are exploring, but proposes no new named defense itself.

title: More than you've asked for: A Comprehensive Analysis of Novel Prompt Injection Threats to Application-Integrated Large Language Models
artifacts_released: Y - synthetic application demos and Bing Chat prompts released at https://github.com/greshake/llm-security and https://github.com/greshake/lm-safety
models_evaluated: Bing Chat (GPT-4-powered) and Bing's code-completion engine (real-world systems); synthetic applications built on GPT-4 and text-davinci-003 (via LangChain and ReAct prompting)
datasets_benchmarks: None original benchmark - the paper uses hand-crafted synthetic applications and local HTML/webpage injections plus live Bing Chat sessions as proof-of-concept demonstrations rather than a standardized benchmark dataset
key_result: Demonstrates practical, working exploits across a security-oriented taxonomy of indirect-prompt-injection impacts - including information gathering/data theft, remote control, persistent cross-session compromise, worming (self-propagating injections that spread the injection to other users/sessions), automated social-engineering/fraud, and search-result manipulation - against both real-world systems (Bing Chat, Bing code completion) and synthetic GPT-4/text-davinci-003 applications, showing that retrieved content can act as arbitrary instruction execution; no aggregate quantitative success-rate metric is reported since the paper is proof-of-concept/qualitative rather than a systematic empirical study.
baselines_compared: None - proof-of-concept demonstration paper with no comparison to a prior attack or defense baseline
threat_model: An adversary who has no direct interface to the LLM application strategically plants prompt-injection payloads in content likely to be retrieved by the LLM (web pages, search results, emails, code repositories, tool outputs), exploiting the application's blurred line between data and instructions to remotely hijack the model's behavior, exfiltrate data, or propagate the injection to other users/sessions (worming) without ever directly prompting the system themselves.

Quantifying attack success rate is acknowledged as methodologically difficult in dynamically evolving, interactive chat sessions and is left to future work; prompt development was noted to be simple and often successful on the first attempt.
technical_summary: Introduces Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI), showing that adversaries can remotely compromise LLM-integrated applications without a direct interface by planting malicious instructions in external content the LLM is likely to retrieve (web pages, search results, emails, code). Derives a security-oriented taxonomy of resulting threats - including data theft, remote control, persistent compromise, information-ecosystem contamination, automated social engineering, and self-propagating 'worm' injections that spread to other users - and demonstrates proof-of-concept exploits against both real-world systems (Bing Chat, Bing code completion) and synthetic GPT-4/text-davinci-003 applications. Discusses several speculative mitigation directions (LLM supervisors/moderators, interpretability-based outlier detection) but explicitly concludes that effective defenses are currently lacking and requires future work.

rq3.name: Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI)
rq3.note: Foundational, extremely widely cited (154 citations) named attack concept: injecting malicious instructions into content an LLM is likely to retrieve, enabling remote compromise without a direct user-facing interface; also introduces the 'prompt injection worm' self-propagating variant.

rq4.note: The 'Mitigations' discussion is explicitly speculative (LLM supervisor/moderator, interpretability-based outlier detection floated as future directions, not implemented, named, or evaluated); the abstract itself states effective mitigations are currently lacking.

title: Prompt Injection Attacks and Defenses in LLM-Integrated Applications
artifacts_released: Y - benchmark platform public at https://github.com/liu00222/Open-Prompt-Injection
models_evaluated: PaLM 2 text-bison-001; Flan-UL2; Vicuna-33b-v1.3; Vicuna-13b-v1.3; GPT-3.5-Turbo; GPT-4 (default); Llama-2-13b-chat; Llama-2-7b-chat; Bard; InternLM-Chat-7B (10 LLMs total)
datasets_benchmarks: 7 tasks (e.g., text summarization, grammar correction, duplicate sentence detection, spam/sentiment/hate-speech-style classification tasks) evaluated across all 7x7 target/injected task combinations, forming the Open-Prompt-Injection benchmark of 5 attacks x 10 defenses x 10 LLMs x 7 tasks
key_result: All 5 formalized prompt injection attacks are effective across LLMs/tasks; the new framework-inspired 'Combined Attack' achieves the largest average Attack Success Value (ASV) among the 5 attacks and outperforms all others for nearly every target/injected task combination (Fake Completion is the runner-up); among the 10 benchmarked defenses, prevention-based defenses show limited effectiveness and/or large utility loss on benign inputs, and only one detection-based defense reliably detects compromised data while the rest miss many attacks - the paper concludes no existing defense is sufficient.
baselines_compared: 5 existing/derived prompt injection attacks (including the new Combined Attack) benchmarked against each other; 10 existing prevention-based and detection-based defenses benchmarked against each other and against a no-defense baseline
threat_model: An attacker controls the external data an LLM-Integrated Application processes (e.g., a resume, a webpage) and appends or embeds an injected instruction/task so that the LLM performs the attacker's injected task instead of, or in addition to, the application's intended target task, without needing direct access to the system prompt.
stated_limitations: All existing prompt injection attacks (including the paper's own Combined Attack) are limited to heuristics such as special characters and fake responses rather than optimization-based methods; the authors explicitly flag developing optimization-based, stronger attacks, new prevention/detection defenses, and post-detection recovery mechanisms as important future work.
technical_summary: Proposes the first framework to formally define and generalize prompt injection attacks against LLM-Integrated Applications, showing that existing published attacks are special cases of this framework, and uses it to design a new 'Combined Attack' that merges multiple existing attack strategies. Conducts the first systematic quantitative benchmark of 5 prompt injection attacks and 10 defenses (5 prevention-based, 5 detection-based) across 10 LLMs and 7 tasks (49 target/injected task combinations), releasing the evaluation platform as Open-Prompt-Injection. Finds all attacks are broadly effective, the Combined Attack is the most effective overall, and that no existing defense adequately balances attack prevention/detection with utility preservation, establishing the benchmark as a baseline for evaluating future prompt-injection attacks and defenses.

rq3.name: Combined Attack
rq3.note: A new, named attack derived from the paper's own formal attack framework by combining multiple existing prompt-injection strategies (e.g., escape characters, context ignoring, fake completion); shown to consistently outperform prior individual attacks across 10 LLMs and 49 task combinations.

rq4.note: The paper formalizes and benchmarks 10 pre-existing defenses (5 prevention-based, 5 detection-based) rather than proposing a new defense of its own; its contribution on the defense side is the benchmark/evaluation framework, not a novel mitigation.

title: Prompt injection attacks on vision language models in oncology
artifacts_released: Y - code available at https://github.com/KatherLab/prompt_injection_attacks under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0
models_evaluated: Claude-3 Opus; Claude-3.5 Sonnet; GPT-4o; Reka Core (all four met the >=50% organ-detection-accuracy inclusion criterion); Gemini 1.5 Plus and Llama-3.1 (405B) were excluded (Gemini's guardrails prevented radiology-image use; Llama-3.1 lacked vision support at the time)
datasets_benchmarks: 18 real, histologically-confirmed malignant-lesion patient cases across 6 imaging modalities (CT, MRI, ultrasound, photography/dermatoscopy, endoscopy, histology), each tested under 3 injection positions x 3 visibility variations (high contrast, low contrast/sub-visual, small font) x 3 replicate iterations, totaling N=594 attacks (72 variations per model x ~3 replicates x 4-5 models, per Supplementary methodology)
key_result: All four evaluated VLMs were susceptible to prompt injection that flipped a correct lesion diagnosis to 'no pathologies': Attack Success Rate was 33% (Claude-3), 40% (Claude-3.5), 67% (GPT-4o), and 51% (Reka Core), each individually significant (p=0.02, 0.01, <0.001, <0.001 respectively) and significant overall (p<0.0001); vulnerability was modality-agnostic, with averaged ASR of 32%, 32%, 49%, 58%, 61% for ultrasound, endoscopy, MRI, CT, and histology respectively; sub-visual (low-contrast/tiny-font) injections were as harmful as visible ones for GPT-4o and Reka Core but markedly less effective against Claude models (e.g., lesion miss rate dropped from 69% to 14% for Claude-3 under low contrast); of three tested mitigations (ethical prompting, a supervisor-agent check, and their combination), only Claude-3.5 showed partial protection, while all others remained largely vulnerable.
baselines_compared: Unaltered (non-injected) prompts serve as the negative-control baseline for measuring lesion miss rate and attack success rate; the paper also compares three ad hoc mitigation conditions (ethical prompt engineering, supervisor-agent check, and their combination) against a default no-mitigation condition
threat_model: A third party with access to a patient's medical image data (but not to the model's parameters) - e.g., via an unprotected CD/DVD import, a compromised hospital IT pipeline, or a third-party VLM-API gateway - embeds a hidden text or sub-visual image instruction telling the VLM to withhold or misreport a cancer diagnosis, exploiting the fact that VLMs cannot distinguish legitimate clinical instructions from adversarial ones injected via text or image content, entirely in a black-box setting without model access.
stated_limitations: Not stated as a dedicated limitations section, but the authors note that Gemini 1.5 Plus's built-in guardrails prevented it from being used on radiology images at all, and that Llama-3.1 (405B), the best available open-source LLM at the time, does not support vision interpretation and so could not be assessed; only VLMs reaching at least 50% organ-detection accuracy were included in subsequent attack experiments, and all attacks were run in a fully simulated (non-clinical, non-live) scenario to prevent real-world harm.
technical_summary: Evaluates prompt injection attacks against vision-language models (VLMs) in a medical oncology context for the first time, using real, histologically-confirmed cancer patient images across six imaging modalities. Tests text-based, visual, and delayed-visual (preceding-image) prompt injection, including sub-visual (low-contrast/tiny-font) variants invisible to human observers, on Claude-3 Opus, Claude-3.5 Sonnet, GPT-4o, and Reka Core, quantifying lesion miss rate and attack success rate across N=594 attacks. Finds all four VLMs can be manipulated into missing an actual malignant lesion, with attack success modality-agnostic and largely unaffected by hiding the injection from human view; also tests and finds largely ineffective three ad hoc mitigation strategies (ethical prompting, a supervisor-agent check, and their combination), with only Claude-3.5 showing partial resistance, and concludes new, specifically designed mitigation techniques are urgently needed before clinical deployment.

rq3.note: Applies existing text- and image-embedded prompt-injection techniques (including sub-visual/steganographic image injection, already known in prior cross-modal prompt-injection literature) to a new, high-stakes domain (oncology VLMs); no fundamentally new attack mechanism is named as the paper's own contribution.

rq4.note: Tests three ad hoc, unnamed mitigation ideas (ethical prompt engineering, a supervisor-agent checker, and their combination) and finds them largely insufficient (only partial effect for Claude-3.5); these are evaluated as informal mitigations, not proposed/characterized as a new named defense contribution.

title: Prompt Injection Attacks on Large Language Models: A Survey of Attack Methods, Root Causes, and Defense Strategies
artifacts_released: N - survey paper, no original artifact
models_evaluated: None - systematic literature review; no original models are run. It synthesizes reported results across 128 peer-reviewed studies (2022-2025).
datasets_benchmarks: None original - the review catalogs datasets/evaluation metrics used across the surveyed literature (Section 6) rather than introducing or running its own
key_result: No original experiment; the review reports synthesized findings across 128 studies: attack sophistication progressed from simple direct injection (2022) to multimodal attacks exceeding 90% success rate against unprotected systems (2024-2025); more capable models show higher vulnerability to text-based attacks (Pearson r=0.6635, p<0.001); across 37 cataloged defense approaches, input-level filtering achieves 60-80% detection with 15-30% false-positive rates, prompt-engineering defenses show 40-60% bypass rates, and advanced architectural defenses reach up to 95% protection against known patterns but leave gaps against novel attacks, with 200-500ms added latency.
baselines_compared: None - descriptive synthesis of results reported by the 128 reviewed primary studies, not an original comparative experiment
threat_model: N/A - reviews threat models used across the surveyed literature (direct, indirect, and multimodal prompt injection targeting system-prompt leakage, behavior hijacking, privilege escalation, and data exfiltration) rather than defining or testing one of its own.
stated_limitations: The review notes that current evaluation methodologies suffer from a lack of standardized metrics across studies, subjective bias in dataset construction, insufficient coverage of multimodal/multilingual scenarios, and limited assessment of defense robustness against adaptive attacks, hindering reproducibility and comparative analysis across the literature it surveys.
technical_summary: Surveys 128 peer-reviewed studies (2022-2025) on prompt injection attacks against LLMs following Kitchenham's systematic literature review guidelines. Constructs a multi-dimensional attack taxonomy (attack vector, attack objective, technical implementation), performs root-cause attribution across philosophical, architectural, and training dimensions, and categorizes 37 existing defense mechanisms into input-preprocessing, system-architecture, and model-level approaches, synthesizing their reported effectiveness and limitations. Also catalogs datasets and evaluation metrics used in the literature. Concludes with research-priority recommendations (formal verification, architectural innovation, standardized evaluation, multimodal defense, human-AI collaborative security) but introduces no original attack, defense, dataset, or experiment of its own.

rq3.note: Systematic literature review; synthesizes and taxonomizes existing attack techniques from 128 surveyed papers without introducing a new named attack of its own.

rq4.note: Systematic literature review; catalogs and characterizes 37 existing defense mechanisms from the surveyed literature without proposing a new named defense.

title: Prompt Injection Detection in LLM Integrated Applications
artifacts_released: N - a data availability statement is present but no code/model/dataset repository link or public release is given
models_evaluated: A fine-tuned BERT classifier as the core ML component of a three-layer detection pipeline (banned-term list, embedding-based similarity search, and BERT classification); evaluated across production use cases at eBay (general, product query, AI assistant, question answering)
datasets_benchmarks: BERT fine-tuning/validation used a combination of open-source prompt-injection datasets (e.g., JasperLS/prompt-injections, ChatGPT-Jailbreak-Prompts, Turkish-Prompt-Injections, and others) and manually curated entries, benchmarked against an unseen ~250k-record validation set
key_result: The fine-tuned BERT model achieves overall accuracy exceeding 0.98 on the ~250k-record validation set with millisecond-scale latency; per-use-case accuracy reaches 0.99 for the largest general-use dataset and about 0.98 for product query, but only 0.91 for the AI-assistant use case due to less diverse training data; all use cases show high recall but comparatively lower precision, indicating a tendency toward false positives.
baselines_compared: None - the three detection layers (banned-term list, embedding similarity search, BERT) are compared against each other's contribution within the pipeline rather than against an external prior detection system
threat_model: A malicious actor submits carefully crafted direct prompts (and, as discussed for future work, indirect prompt injections via retrieved URL content) to an LLM-integrated production application to manipulate model responses for purposes such as extracting sensitive information, introducing bias, or compromising downstream application/API integrity.
stated_limitations: The paper identifies unresolved challenges rather than closing them: balancing security (low false-negative rate) against usability (low false-positive rate, low latency) is difficult, especially as larger/more accurate models increase response latency; the AI-assistant use case shows notably lower accuracy (0.91) due to limited training-data diversity; the current system is not yet equipped to detect LLM outputs being weaponized against downstream services (e.g., generating XSS/SQL-injection payloads) or to perform deep content analysis of URLs/linked content for indirect prompt injection, both flagged as future work.
technical_summary: Presents a production-oriented, three-layer detection system for prompt injection in LLM-integrated applications (eBay), combining a predefined banned-term list, embedding-based similarity search, and a fine-tuned BERT classifier to identify and neutralize malicious inputs in real time. Benchmarks the BERT component on an unseen ~250k-record validation set spanning multiple real production use cases (general, product query, AI assistant, question answering), achieving overall accuracy above 0.98 with millisecond latency, though accuracy drops to 0.91 for the less-data-rich AI-assistant use case, and all use cases show a precision-recall imbalance favoring recall. Discusses open challenges around the security-usability-latency tradeoff and the need for future work on detecting indirect prompt injection via retrieved URL content and on preventing LLM outputs from being weaponized against downstream systems.

rq3.note: No new attack technique is introduced; the paper discusses known direct and (as future work) indirect prompt-injection threats without naming a new mechanism.

rq4.note: The three-layer pipeline (banned-term list + embedding similarity search + fine-tuned BERT) is a combination of standard, individually well-known techniques rather than a distinctly named system; the paper does not give its overall approach a name or characterize the combination itself as a novel architectural contribution beyond an applied production deployment.
